title: Input, Output & Programs
subtitle: This week covers how Python communicates with the user — the print() function for output and input() for reading user data. Type conversion is critical: everything from input() comes as a string and must be converted before arithmetic.
learningOutcome: This week covers how Python communicates with the user — the print() function for output and input() for reading user data. Type conversion is critical: everything from input() comes as a string and must be converted before arithmetic.

content.text: print() displays output to the screen. Can print text (strings), numbers, variables, and expressions.
print("Hello, ECE 220!") # Output: Hello, ECE 220! name = "Mumuni" age = 3 print("Name:", name, "Year:", age) # Name: Mumuni Year: 3 print("2 + 2 =", 2 + 2) # 2 + 2 = 4

content.text: input() pauses the program and waits for the user to type something. It ALWAYS returns a string.

Common mistake — Trying to do arithmetic directly on an input() result: age = input ( "Enter your age: " ) next_year = age + 1 # TypeError! Can't add string and int Fix with type conversion: age = int ( input ( "Enter your age: " )) next_year = age + 1 # Works: 22 if age is 21

content.text: int() converts to integer. float() converts to decimal. str() converts to string.

test_score = float(input("Enter test score: ")) assignment_score = float(input("Enter assignment score: ")) attendance = float(input("Enter attendance %: ")) final = (test_score + (2 * assignment_score)) / 3 + (5 if attendance >= 90 else 0) print("Final Score:", final)

content.text: Shorthand for if/else in one line: value_if_true if condition else value_if_false
bonus = 5 if attendance >= 90 else 0 # Same as: # if attendance >= 90: # bonus = 5 # else: # bonus = 0

Key fact — write this verbatim:
input() always returns a string. You must use int() or float() to convert it before arithmetic.
